title: Environment & Exported Variables 🌍
description: Learn the difference between shell and environment variables, and how to pass data to child processes.

slides.title: Shell vs. Environment Variables 🔄
slides.content:
## Two Scopes

- **Shell variables** exist only in the current shell session. If you run a script or a new shell, they aren't visible.
- **Environment variables** are passed to child processes (subshells, scripts, commands).

Every shell variable starts as a shell variable. To promote it to environment, use `export`.

quizData.question: What keyword makes a variable available to child processes?
quizData.explanation: The `export` command turns a shell variable into an environment variable, visible to subprocesses.

slides.title: Common Environment Variables 📋
slides.content:
## Built‑in Goodies

- `HOME` – your home directory.
- `USER` – your username.
- `PATH` – directories searched for commands.
- `SHELL` – path to your current shell.
- `PWD` – current working directory (usually).

You can view all environment variables with `env` or `printenv`.

quizData.question: Which environment variable holds your username?
quizData.explanation: `$USER` (or `$LOGNAME`) typically stores the current user's name.

slides.title: How Export Works ⚙️
slides.content:
## Export at Assignment

You can export and assign in one step:
```bash
export VAR=value
```
Or later:
```bash
VAR=value
export VAR
```

**Remember**: changes to an environment variable in a child do **not** affect the parent.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Keep It Clean
Avoid exporting too many variables; it can pollute the environment and cause unexpected behaviour in other programs.
